title: Sodium — Extraction, Properties and Uses
topicTitle: Sodium: extraction from Down's process, properties and uses
notes: **Downs cell design:** The industrial extraction of sodium by electrolysis of molten NaCl uses the Downs cell, invented by James C. Downs in 1924. The cell consists of a steel outer container (cathode compartment) with an iron cathode at the center, surrounded by a cylindrical graphite anode. A wire gauze diaphragm separates the anode and cathode compartments to prevent mixing of Na and Cl₂. The cell operates at 600°C with a voltage of 7–8 V and current of 25,000–40,000 A.

**Why CaCl₂ is added to NaCl:** Pure NaCl melts at 801°C, but sodium metal vaporizes at 883°C, creating dangerous pressure and sodium loss. Adding CaCl₂ (40% NaCl + 60% CaCl₂ by weight) forms a eutectic mixture that melts at ~600°C — well below sodium's boiling point. This eutectic also has good electrical conductivity and lower viscosity, improving current efficiency from ~25% (pure NaCl) to ~95%. The Ca²⁺ ions are not discharged because Na⁺ has a less negative reduction potential in this melt.

**Electrolysis reactions in Downs cell:** At cathode (iron): Na⁺ + e⁻ → Na(l) — sodium metal forms and rises to the collection chamber. At anode (graphite): 2Cl⁻ → Cl₂(g) + 2e⁻ — chlorine gas is collected separately. Overall: 2NaCl(l) → 2Na(l) + Cl₂(g). The chlorine is a valuable co-product used in PVC production, water treatment, and bleach manufacture. A small amount of Ca is also produced at the cathode (~0.2%) but is re-oxidized by Cl₂ before it can contaminate the sodium.

**Sodium collection and storage:** Molten sodium (density 0.927 g/cm³ at 100°C) rises because it is less dense than the molten NaCl-CaCl₂ electrolyte (density ~1.5 g/cm³). It is collected in a stainless steel bell above the cathode and transferred under dry argon atmosphere to storage containers. The sodium is kept under paraffin oil or dry kerosene to prevent oxidation. Even trace moisture causes rapid tarnishing and hydrogen evolution.

**Physical properties of sodium:** Soft silvery-white metal (Mohs hardness 0.5 — can be cut with a knife). Density: 0.971 g/cm³ at 20°C (less dense than water, floats). Melting point: 97.8°C, boiling point: 883°C. Good conductor of electricity (3.8 × 10⁷ S/m, about 30% that of copper). Thermal conductivity: 142 W/m·K. Sodium's low melting point and high thermal conductivity make it an excellent coolant for nuclear reactors (fast breeder reactors use liquid sodium to transfer heat from the core).

**Reaction with water:** 2Na(s) + 2H₂O(l) → 2NaOH(aq) + H₂(g). This is a vigorous exothermic reaction (ΔH = −184 kJ/mol). The sodium melts into a ball (heat of reaction exceeds its melting point), darts across the water surface, and the hydrogen may ignite with a lilac flame (from sodium vapor excitation). The resulting solution is strongly alkaline (NaOH). The reaction is less violent than potassium's because sodium's higher melting point keeps it as a solid ball longer, limiting surface area.

**Reaction with oxygen:** Sodium reacts with oxygen to form different products depending on conditions: (1) Limited oxygen, room temperature: 4Na + O₂ → 2Na₂O (sodium oxide, white solid). (2) Excess oxygen, burning: 2Na + O₂ → Na₂O₂ (sodium peroxide, pale yellow solid). (3) In pure oxygen: NaO₂ (sodium superoxide) can form under high pressure. Sodium oxide reacts with water to form NaOH; sodium peroxide reacts with water to form NaOH and H₂O₂. Na₂O₂ is a powerful oxidizing agent used in breathing apparatus and as a bleaching agent.

**Reaction with acids:** Sodium reacts violently with dilute acids: 2Na + 2HCl → 2NaCl + H₂. The reaction is more violent than with water because the acid provides a higher concentration of H⁺ ions. The reaction is so exothermic that the hydrogen produced often ignites immediately. Sodium is NEVER used to generate hydrogen in the laboratory because the reaction is too dangerous — zinc or aluminum with dilute acid is preferred.

**Reaction with ammonia:** Sodium dissolves in liquid ammonia to form a deep blue solution containing solvated electrons: Na + (x)NH₃ → Na⁺(NH₃)x + e⁻(NH₃)x. The blue color is due to the absorption of light by the solvated electrons. On standing, the solution slowly releases hydrogen: 2Na + 2NH₃ → 2NaNH₂ + H₂ (sodium amide forms). The solution is a strong reducing agent — it can reduce alkynes to trans-alkenes (dissolved metal reduction). Concentrated solutions appear bronze-colored and conduct electricity like a metal.

**Reaction with hydrogen:** 2Na + H₂ → 2NaH (sodium hydride) at 360–400°C. NaH is a saline (ionic) hydride containing H⁻ ions. It is a non-existent in water: NaH + H₂O → NaOH + H₂. NaH is used as a strong base and reducing agent in organic synthesis (e.g., deprotonation of alcohols, formation of alkoxides). It is also used in the manufacture of sodium borohydride (NaBH₄), an important reducing agent in organic chemistry.

**Reaction with halogens:** 2Na + Cl₂ → 2NaCl (vigorous, yellow flame). Na reacts with Br₂ and I₂ similarly, though the reaction with I₂ is less vigorous (lower oxidizing power of I₂). NaCl is the most important product — it is the raw material for the chlor-alkali industry. The reaction is so exothermic that it is used as a model for teaching thermochemistry. NaCl has a lattice energy of 787 kJ/mol and a melting point of 801°C.

**Uses of sodium:** (1) Sodium-vapour lamps — produce characteristic yellow light (589 nm D-lines) for street lighting; modern high-pressure lamps produce whiter light. (2) Na-Pb alloy (Na 2–10%) used as an anti-knock agent in gasoline (phased out due to lead toxicity). (3) Liquid sodium coolant in fast breeder nuclear reactors (PHWR, BN-600) because of its high thermal conductivity and low neutron absorption cross-section. (4) Reducing agent in the extraction of Ti (from TiCl₄), Zr (from ZrCl₄), and other transition metals. (5) NaK alloy (77% K, 23% Na) is liquid at room temperature and used as a heat transfer fluid.

**Production statistics:** Global sodium production is approximately 150,000 tonnes/year (2023), with China, the US, and India as the largest producers. The energy cost is ~11–13 kWh per kg of sodium. The cost of sodium metal is approximately $1–2/kg, making it economically viable for specialized applications but too expensive for bulk structural use (compared to aluminium at ~$2/kg for primary production). Most sodium is consumed in the manufacture of sodium compounds (Na₂S, NaCN, NaNO₂) rather than used as the metal itself.

**Safety considerations:** Sodium fires cannot be extinguished with water (2Na + 2H₂O → 2NaOH + H₂, the H₂ ignites). Class D fire extinguishers (dry powder, Class D agent) or sand must be used. Sodium burns produce intense yellow flames and caustic NaOH spray. Skin contact with sodium causes severe chemical burns (NaOH formation) and thermal burns. Storage must be in airtight containers under oil, away from water sources and oxidizing agents.
confusion: Why CaCl₂ and not another salt: CaCl₂ is chosen because Ca²⁺ has a more positive (less negative) reduction potential than Na⁺, so calcium does not deposit at the cathode. Other salts like KCl would co-deposit potassium (similar reduction potential), contaminating the sodium. NaCa alloy formation is minimized by the specific eutectic composition. The 40:60 NaCl:CaCl₂ ratio gives the lowest melting point (~600°C) while maintaining good conductivity.

Sodium vs. potassium reactivity with water: Students often assume potassium is always more reactive than sodium. While potassium reacts MORE VIOLENTLY with water (the H₂ ignites immediately), sodium is still very reactive (melts, darts, may ignite). The key difference is that sodium's higher melting point (98°C vs. K's 63°C) means it takes longer to melt and expose fresh surface, making the sodium reaction appear slightly less violent. However, both are far more reactive than lithium.

Sodium-vapour lamps are NOT 'sodium lights' in the decorative sense: Low-pressure sodium lamps produce nearly monochromatic yellow light (589 nm) — everything appears yellow or grey. High-pressure sodium lamps produce a broader spectrum (golden-white) and are more common in modern installations. Neither is suitable for applications where color discrimination is needed (art galleries, surgery) because the narrow emission spectrum renders all colors as shades of yellow.

NaK alloy is liquid but reactive: NaK (77% K, 23% Na) is liquid at room temperature (melting point −12.6°C) and is used as a heat transfer fluid in specialized nuclear reactors. However, it is PYROPHORIC — it ignites spontaneously in air and reacts violently with water. It must be handled in argon atmosphere. This is different from the Na-Pb alloy, which is stable in air.

Sodium is NOT used for hydrogen generation in labs: The reaction 2Na + 2HCl → 2NaCl + H₂ is too violent and dangerous for laboratory hydrogen generation. Zinc (Zn + H₂SO₄ → ZnSO₄ + H₂) or aluminum (2Al + 3H₂SO₄ → Al₂(SO₄)₃ + 3H₂) are preferred because they react at a controllable rate. Sodium's extreme reactivity makes it impossible to moderate the reaction in a simple lab setup.
practice: Calculate the mass of sodium and volume of chlorine gas (at STP) produced when a Downs cell operates at 25,000 A for 24 hours. Use Faraday's law: m = MIt/nF. (Expected: ~129 kg Na, ~40.5 m³ Cl₂.) If the cell operates at 7.5 V, calculate the electrical energy consumed in kWh and the cost at $0.08/kWh.

Explain why the eutectic composition of 40% NaCl + 60% CaCl₂ melts at 600°C while pure NaCl melts at 801°C. Draw a qualitative phase diagram showing the eutectic point. Calculate the moles of CaCl₂ and NaCl in 1 kg of eutectic mixture and the expected density of the melt (assume additive volumes: NaCl density 2.17 g/cm³, CaCl₂ density 2.15 g/cm³).

Describe the correct procedure using Class D extinguishing agents (dry powder, graphite powder, or sand). Write the chemical equations showing why each wrong extinguisher would make the fire worse.

Calculate the theoretical energy cost (in kWh) to produce 1 tonne of sodium from NaCl by electrolysis. Given that the actual Downs cell consumes 11–13 kWh/kg, calculate the current efficiency. Explain why the efficiency is not 100% (consider sodium re-dissolving in the melt, Na-Cl recombination, and side reactions with Ca²⁺).

universalFacts: The total amount of sodium produced worldwide (150,000 tonnes/year) is tiny compared to aluminium (70 million tonnes/year), yet sodium is essential for several irreplaceable applications. No alternative process exists for producing titanium metal (Kroll process uses sodium as the reducing agent), and liquid sodium coolant is unmatched for heat transfer in fast breeder reactors.

Sodium-vapour lamps have illuminated streets since the 1930s. The first high-pressure sodium lamp was developed in 1964 by General Electric. Modern high-pressure sodium lamps achieve 100–150 lumens per watt, making them one of the most energy-efficient light sources available. The global market for sodium lamps is approximately $2 billion/year.

The Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase pump in human cells consumes approximately 20–40% of the body's ATP at rest — more than any other single cellular process. This is why sodium and potassium balance is critical for health. The medical condition hyperkalemia (high blood potassium) can be fatal because it disrupts the electrochemical gradient needed for heart function.

Sodium's use as a nuclear reactor coolant dates to the 1950s. The Experimental Breeder Reactor I (EBR-I) in Idaho, USA, was the first power reactor to generate electricity from sodium-cooled fast breeder technology (1951). Today, Russia's BN-800 reactor (800 MW thermal) and China's CEFR use liquid sodium to cool the core, demonstrating the technology's maturity and reliability.

Sodium was first isolated by Humphry Davy in 1807 by electrolysis of molten NaOH. He obtained so little sodium that he could not weigh it — he described it as 'a small globule' with metallic luster. Davy also isolated potassium (from KOH) in the same experiment, marking the birth of electrochemistry and the discovery of entire new groups of elements.
